problem.title: Repeat bearing and mechanical seal failures on slurry pump P-101
problem.whatHappened: P-101 slurry feed pump failed 6 times in 12 months (3 mechanical seal, 3 bearing), losing 84 hours of production and costing $238,440 per year in lost margin and repair.
problem.where: Drive-end and non-drive-end bearings and the mechanical seal of P-101, a single slurry feed pump with no standby.
problem.when: Spread across all shifts and seasons over the last 12 months: 3 mechanical seal events and 3 bearing events.
problem.impact: There is no buffer capacity, so a pump stop is a line stop and lost hours are lost production hours. Each failure takes 14 hours to diagnose, isolate, drain, rebuild and restart, losing 1,680 tonnes at 120 t/h, which is $30,240 of margin plus $9,500 of repair. Secondary damage, overtime premium, delayed planned work and environmental clean-up are not counted, so the real loss is higher.

evidence.title: A1: DCS flow trend, discharge valve log and pump curve overlay
evidence.note: Flow sits at about 60% of best efficiency flow for most operating hours. The pump is run away from the point it was selected for. Discharge valve position log shows it throttled most of the time.

evidence.title: A2: Bearing race wear track, soft foot check, maintenance history search
evidence.note: Off-centre wear track on the bearing races, typical of misalignment. One foot lifts when its bolt is loosened. No alignment record exists for 4 of the 6 rebuilds.

evidence.title: A3: Oil samples at teardown, housing seal and breather inspection
evidence.note: Water and solids found in the oil at teardown. Housing seals are worn and the breather vent is open to wash-down.

evidence.title: B1: Seal face inspection, flush flow reading, strainer inspection
evidence.note: Seal faces scored and heat cracked (ran dry or hot). Measured flush flow is below design. Strainer found packed with solids.

evidence.title: B3: Rebuild job cards and fitter interview
evidence.note: No set length is recorded on any of the 3 seal rebuild cards. Fitters set the seal by experience.

evidence.title: Root 1: Throughput change history, impeller size vs current duty, change records
evidence.note: Throughput changed with no pump duty review on file. The impeller is oversized for the current duty.

evidence.title: Root 2: Work instructions and training records
evidence.note: No document states an alignment method, tolerance or record. No laser tool on site and no training records.

evidence.title: Root 3: Review of the rebuild procedure
evidence.note: No seal setting step, no soft foot check, and housing seals are reused.

evidence.title: Root 4: Job close-out records
evidence.note: The pump was returned to service without an alignment or vibration reading.

evidence.title: Root 5: Inspection route and PM list
evidence.note: Neither flush flow nor oil condition appears on any inspection route.

evidence.title: Root 6: Maintenance system history
evidence.note: Six events were logged under two generic codes (bearing failure, seal failure) with no cause field filled, so the repeat pattern was invisible.

tree.text: Repeat bearing and mechanical seal failures on P-101

children.text: A. Bearings fail early
A1. Pump runs at about 60% of best efficiency flow, so radial load on the shaft is high
Operators throttle the discharge valve to match downstream demand
ROOT 1: Pump duty was never reviewed after throughput changed; impeller is oversized for current duty; no management-of-change trigger for duty changes
A2. Coupling misalignment and a soft foot after rebuilds
Fitters align by straight edge and feel; soft foot is not checked
ROOT 2: No precision alignment standard (method, tolerance, record), no laser tool, fitters not trained
ROOT 4: No verification after repair (alignment record, vibration reading) before handover
A3. Bearing oil contaminated with water and solids (worn housing seals, open breather)
Wash-down hose aimed at bearing housings; oil topped up from open containers
ROOT 3: Rebuild procedure gaps: reuses worn housing seals, no sealed-breather or isolator standard, no soft foot check
ROOT 5b: Oil condition not on any inspection route
B. Mechanical seals fail early
B1. Seal faces run dry or hot because flush flow is restricted (strainer packed, flush valve part closed)
Flush strainer not checked; flush valve position not verified after maintenance
ROOT 5a: Flush is on no inspection route; no flow indicator or low-flow alarm
B2. Seal faces and sleeve see excess shaft movement
Driven by A1 (off best efficiency point) and A2 (misalignment); same roots 1, 2 and 4
B3. Seal set length not controlled on rebuild
Seal set by experience, not recorded
ROOT 3 (again): rebuild procedure has no seal setting step or check
C. Cross-cutting: failures are not recorded in a way that shows the pattern
ROOT 6: Failures coded only as "bearing failure" or "seal failure" in the maintenance system, so the repeat pattern and causes were invisible

actions.description: Trim impeller / re-rate duty so the operating point sits near best efficiency (needs shutdown)
Upgrade seal flush: flow indicator, clean strainer, add to inspection route
Write alignment standard, buy laser alignment tool, train fitters (standard week 4, training week 8)

Fit bearing housing isolators and sealed breathers; write rebuild checklist with seal setting, soft foot check, alignment record and vibration reading before handover. Also fixes Roots 4 and 5b, see the next two lines; cost counted once here
Require alignment record and vibration reading before handover (part of the action above, cost included there)
Add oil condition check to the inspection route (part of the action above, cost included there)
Engineering and project time across all actions
Add pump duty to the management-of-change checklist
Add cause and failure-mode fields to repair coding
Effectiveness check: report failures, hours and cost at 90 days and 12 months
actions.owner: Reliability engineer, reported to plant manager

verification.notes: Failures measured over 12 months after the actions: 1 per year, down from 6. Cost and hours per event are held at the same values as before so the comparison is fair. Capacity released: 70 hours, 8,400 tonnes, $151,200 of margin plus $47,500 of repair cost avoided, which equals the $198,700 annual saving. Simple payback ignores the time value of money, tax and cost of capital. All figures are illustrative.
